#7536. The Supreme Court and profanity

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

Each weekday, we present news articles and commentary related to the Supreme Court in a smart, approachable way.

Free readers receive the Friday edition. Full access is for members.

A written companion to Advisory Opinions, bringing together each episode’s key arguments, takeaways, show notes, and source material on the Supreme Court, the Constitution, and the law.

Coverage and analysis of Supreme Court opinion announcements.

Professor Akhil Reed Amar, joined by co-host Andy Lipka, offers weekly in-depth discussions on the most urgent and fascinating constitutional issues of our day.

Divided Argument is an unscheduled, unpredictable Supreme Court podcast hosted by Will Baude and Dan Epps.

Around 2 p.m. on October 30, 1973, John Douglas was driving with his 15-year-old son when he heard a litany of profanity come over the radio. New York’s WBAI, a nonprofit radio station, was airing a program on modern attitudes toward language. Near the end, the station played George Carlin’s “Filthy Words” routine, which begins with the comedian saying he’d been thinking about “the words you couldn’t say on the public airwaves; the ones you definitely wouldn’t say, ever.” He went on to repeat those words several times, contrasting them with words like “bastards,” “hell,” and “damn,” which were mostly acceptable, and showing how even some of his list of seven were perfectly fine in other contexts. His point was to show the absurdity of profanity.

The station later said it had chosen Carlin’s routine because it was an “incisive satirical view of the subject under discussion,” in the style of other great satirists like Mark Twain or Mort Sahl. Carlin, the station explained, was doing more than “mouthing obscenities.” He was “using words to satirize as harmless and essentially silly our attitudes towards those words.”

Before playing the routine, the host had warned that it included language some listeners might find offensive and suggested they return in 15 minutes if they were inclined toward offense. But about a month later, John Douglas complained to the Federal Communications Commission about the transmission which he said was “garbage” and had been broadcast in the presence of his “young son.” He was the only listener to do so. A member of Morality in Media who frequently listened to the station to “see how far” they’d go, Douglas later acknowledged that he had laughed out loud at the bit but “did not appreciate WBIA’s ‘smart-alecky’ on-air provocations.”

The previous year, Carlin had been arrested after performing an earlier version of the same routine, but a judge threw out the charge. This time, the FCC found the broadcast “indecent,” and put its order in the station’s license file.

That order ended up before the Supreme Court.

Early in its order, the FCC acknowledged that Congress had forbade it from censoring broadcasts. But Congress had also prohibited the broadcast of “obscene, indecent, or profane” language, and the Commission thought Carlin’s broadcast fit the bill. In the FCC’s view, the ban on “indecent” language covered not just obscenity, but also patently offensive language when there was a reasonable risk of children listening. Late at night, when children were unlikely to be listening, the same material might be okay if it appeared in a work of serious literary, artistic, political, or scientific value.

Two commissioners thought even that was too permissive. Charlotte Reid believed “this language to be totally inappropriate for broadcast at anytime” and thought the commission’s standard did “not go far enough.” Commissioner James Quello took much the same view. “Garbage is garbage,” he wrote, whether children were listening or not.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit, however, set aside the order in a 2-1 vote, with one judge believing it violated the statutory ban on censorship and the other saying it violated the First Amendment. The FCC appealed to the Supreme Court.

At oral argument, which was held in April of 1978, several justices made their distaste for Carlin’s bit plain. When Pacifica’s lawyer stressed that the station had warned listeners beforehand and aired the monologue as part of an educational program about language, Chief Justice Warren Burger incredulously asked, “This is educational in your view?” And when counsel defended the material’s artistic value, Justice Thurgood Marshall responded, “Well, I’m not an expert, but if that’s artistic, deliver me.” Justice William Rehnquist, for his part, tested the limits of Pacifica’s position with a hypothetical involving a single four-letter word repeated for an hour. Would the FCC be powerless to prohibit that? Justice John Paul Stevens, however, seemed troubled by the potential reach of the FCC’s position, given that the prohibition on indecency could be enforced through criminal law.

One striking exchange concerned the Justice Department’s position to argue separately, and more narrowly, than the FCC. The solicitor general’s office urged that the First Amendment prevented the government from barring particular words outright for a substantial part of the day without regard to context, even if the FCC could constitutionally regulate “indecency” to some extent. Rehnquist sharply asked why the Justice Department was arguing against the FCC, what interest it had in seeking a narrow construction of an act of Congress, and whether the solicitor general, as the government’s lawyer, could ever argue that an act of Congress was unconstitutional.

Justice Lewis Powell also pressed the DOJ on the reasons behind its departure from the FCC, noting that the DOJ had supported the FCC in the court below. “That is true, and that is an embarrassment to us,” Deputy Solicitor General Louis Claiborne acknowledged, suggesting it was because the matter had been handled there by the Antitrust Division rather than the Criminal Division. Another explanation, which he did not mention, was that the administration had changed.

The court ultimately ruled 5-4 that the FCC could constitutionally treat this broadcast as “indecent” under the governing statute, and that the government could constitutionally prohibit indecency even though it fell short of legal obscenity. Stevens wrote for Burger, Justice Harry Blackmun, Powell, and Rehnquist, having apparently struggled with the case and flip-flopped before settling against Pacifica. The Commission had treated the piece as a nuisance, and, as the court had observed in Village of Euclid v. Ambler Realty Co., a nuisance could be as simple as “a pig in the parlor instead of the barnyard.” He concluded that “when the Commission finds that a pig has entered the parlor, the exercise of its regulatory power does not depend on proof that the pig is obscene.” Though the holding expanded the government’s power to regulate speech, Stevens emphasized broadcasting’s pervasive presence in the home and its accessibility to children, the fact the piece was broadcast during the daytime, and the narrowness of the holding. He did not address late night broadcasts or the “occasional expletive.”

Stevens had only three votes for some parts of his opinion. Powell, joined by Blackmun, wrote separately to object to Stevens’ suggestion that the level of protection that speech receives should depend on a judge’s perception of that speech’s value. For them, the combination of repeated, patently offensive language, an afternoon broadcast, and children’s ready access was enough to resolve the case. Powell also addressed the concern that the decision could end up “reduc[ing] the adult population . . . to [hearing] only what is fit for children”: adults could buy tapes or hear the same words at theaters.

Justice Potter Stewart dissented, joined by Justices William Brennan, Byron White, and Marshall. Stewart would have resolved the case on statutory grounds. He read “indecent” to reach only obscene material, and everyone agreed that Carlin’s monologue fell outside that category. His opinion recalled his concurrence in Jacobellis v. Ohio, where he voted to overturn an obscenity conviction for showing a French film with an explicit love scene. Stewart understood obscenity narrowly, but declined to define it, famously observing in that case, “I know it when I see it, and the motion picture involved in this case is not that.”

Brennan wrote a separate dissent, joined by Marshall, that went further. He agreed with Stewart on the statute and said he would ordinarily refrain from addressing the constitutional question, but he found “the Court’s misapplication of fundamental First Amendment principles so patent, and its attempt to impose its notions of propriety on the whole of the American people so misguided,” that he was “unable to remain silent.”

Brennan disputed the analogy between a radio broadcast and an intrusion into the home. Listeners voluntarily turn on the radio, and they can voluntarily turn it off. In perhaps his sharpest passage, he wrote:

Brennan also questioned the majority’s reliance on protecting children. He read the court’s precedents as allowing the government to shield children from material that was obscene as to them. In his view, Carlin’s routine fell outside that category. Keeping it off the radio during the afternoon cut off access for adults as well as children. And while the majority had invoked parents’ right to raise their children as they saw fit, Brennan thought the FCC had somewhat ironically made the choice for them.

Finally, he remained unconvinced that the court’s reasoning would reach only cases like Carlin’s. Among the things it could sweep in were “literary works, novels, poems, and plays by the likes of Shakespeare, Joyce, Hemingway, Ben Jonson, Henry Fielding, Robert Burns, and Chaucer,” “a good deal of political speech, such as the Nixon tapes,” and even portions of the Bible. In his view, the public, and not the court, should have the power to weed out “worthless and offensive” speech in a marketplace “unsullied by the censor’s hand.”

Brennan and Marshall had joined together in another Supreme Court opinion involving the F-word. In Cohen v. California, they joined Justice John Harlan II’s opinion protecting the right to wear a jacket emblazoned with “Fuck the Draft.” Stewart joined it too (not surprisingly, Burger and Blackmun dissented). Brennan brought Cohen straight into his Pacifica dissent; as he made clear, changing the words can change what the speaker communicates, something that applies especially well to Carlin because the taboo words were themselves the subject of the routine. And Brennan thought telling listeners to buy a record or pay to see Carlin live missed what it meant to hear the routine on the radio.

In closing, Brennan wrote that the majority had only “confirm[ed] Carlin’s prescience as a social commentator.” (It was interesting that Marshall, who sounded distinctly unimpressed by the claim of artistic merit at oral argument, joined him, perhaps especially here.) As Brennan pointed out, Carlin had made fun of the rules about which words you could say on the air, and the court had exemplified the very attitude he was satirizing. To top it all off: Appended to the opinion is the transcript of Carlin’s routine, giving his “indecent” words a permanent home in the U.S. Reports.

At the 2002 Billboard Music Awards on Fox, Cher dispatched the critics who’d spent decades predicting her downfall with “So f*** ’em.” At the 2003 awards, Nicole Richie asked whether anyone had tried getting cow manure out of a Prada purse, then used the F-word to describe how hard it was. The next year, after Bono called U2’s Golden Globe win “really, really f***ing brilliant,” the FCC announced that even a single expletive could be indecent, and it later applied that approach to the two earlier Fox broadcasts.

In 2009, the Supreme Court took up the dispute in FCC v. Fox Television Stations. Writing for a 5-4 majority, Justice Antonin Scalia held that the FCC had adequately explained its change in policy under the Administrative Procedure Act, leaving the First Amendment question open. Justice Clarence Thomas joined the majority but wrote separately to question Pacifica’s holding. On remand, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 2nd Circuit struck down the policy as unconstitutionally vague.

The case returned to the Supreme Court in 2012 and all eight participating justices agreed on the result (Justice Sonia Sotomayor recused herself). Justice Anthony Kennedy’s opinion held that the FCC had failed to give Fox fair notice that fleeting expletives could trigger an indecency finding, but once again left both Pacifica and the First Amendment question open. Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg wrote separately to say that Pacifica was wrong from the start and deserved reconsideration. But while the court has had several cases involving curse words since, it has yet to take up the question directly.

In 2004, the FCC dismissed complaints related to the airing of Saving Private Ryan on the basis that the film’s curse words helped convey the soldiers’ experience. But just two years later, it slapped a station with $15,000 in fines for airing a Martin Scorsese documentary about Blues music that contained profanity. In 2020, the FCC received over 1,300 complaints about Jennifer Lopez and Shakira’s halftime show, though it never took any action against the network. And in February 2026, FCC requested transcripts of Bad Bunny’s Superbowl halftime performance before ultimately finding no violation.

Half a century after Carlin’s seven dirty words, the FCC’s continued and seemingly arbitrary application of its indecency laws shows the prescience of Brennan’s dissent and the need to finally answer the question of whether the Constitution prohibits the “dominant culture” from trying to force “groups who do not share its mores to conform to its way of acting, thinking, and speaking.”

Anastasia Boden is a Senior Attorney at the Pacific Legal Foundation, where she brings civil rights lawsuits that advance the Constitution’s promises of equality and economic opportunity.

#7535. Virginia Supreme Court rules state unconstitutionally disarmed nonviolent felon

The petitioner brought an as-applied, not facial, challenge, but criminal defense experts said the ruling opens the door to a flood of Second Amendment-based challenges to Virginia's felon-in-possession law.

RICHMOND, Va. (CN) â When police responded to a domestic dispute in Frederick County, Virginia, Derek Ginevan, a felon with previous convictions for drug offenses and larceny, admitted to possessing a shotgun â an admission that landed him a three-year prison sentence.

The Supreme Court of Virginia unanimously ruled Wednesday that the stateâs law prohibiting felons like Ginevan from exercising their Second Amendment right runs afoul of the U.S. Constitution and fails the historical tradition of firearms regulations analysis the Supreme Court created in New York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen. Virginia permanently bans felons from possessing firearms unless they petition a court to have their right restored.

The ruling reverses the Virginia Court of Appeals’ judgment, which held that the circuit court properly sentenced Ginevan, albeit for different reasons. The circuit court determined that felons are not “the people” referenced in the Second Amendment. Justice Wesley Russell Jr. said the determination was error.

“The fact that the phrase ‘right of the people’ means the same thing in the First, Fourth and Second Amendments is, by our reckoning, sufficient to resolve whether a felony conviction, without more, removes a person from the political community,” Russell said. “Because a felony conviction does not remove a person from ’the people’ referenced in the First and Fourth Amendments, we conclude that, as a matter of language and logic, it does not remove a person from ’the people’ referenced in the Second Amendment."

The Court of Appeals assumed Ginevan was included as part of “the people” but ruled Ginevan’s 2018 conviction for possessing ammunition is a violent felony under state law. The Court of Appeals then examined the nation’s historic traditions and observed that the United States has long barred those judged to pose a danger to the public from possessing firearms. The Supreme Court of Virginia, however, ruled no founding-era law permanently disarmed nonincarcerated people based on a felony conviction.

“Statutes banning convicted felons from possessing firearms as a result of their prior felony convictions are a creature of 20th-century legislatures,” Russell said. “The inability of the commonwealth to offer even one example from the relevant timeframe of a statute barring all felons or even violent felons from possessing even a class of firearms, let alone all firearms and ammunition, is a significant strike against the constitutionality of Code Â§ 18.2-308.2.”

Shawn Weneta, director of government affairs at Cavalier Consulting, who himself regained his Second Amendment right in January, said the laws banning possession come from the Jim Crow era.

“Once we started saying it’s okay to strip people of their rights because of a criminal conviction, and then started, you know, criminalizing Black culture, we became very much desensitized,” Weneta said in an interview.

Executive Director of Justice Forward Virginia Brad Haywood said the felon-in-possession law disproportionately impacts Black people.

“If you’re Black in America, you’re much more likely to have a felony conviction,” Haywood said during an interview. “So I think this has also just a disproportionate positive impact on them.”

In affirming Ginevan’s conviction, the Court of Appeals observed English laws denying firearms to those who declined to join the Church of England or colonial laws disarming Native Americans. Russell ruled the laws aren’t analogous because they disarmed those viewed as disloyal to the state rather than punishing crimes.

Haywood said he doesn’t expect the ruling to impact the restoration of civil rights, like the right to hold public office or serve on a jury. Weneta said he’s interested to see how Virginia’s Democratic-led General Assembly approaches the ruling during the 2027 session. Weneta noted the ruling intersects the interests of criminal justice reform and Second Amendment advocates.

“I think there are quite a few very interesting questions now in front of advocates, you know, Second Amendment advocates, gun control advocates, very interesting questions in front of legislators, and of course a very interesting question in front of the attorney general,” Weneta said.

The Office of Attorney General Jay Jones did not respond to a request for comment. Attorney Elliot Harding said he expects a flood of habeas corpus petitions from people currently serving time for felon-in-possession offenses, but he doubts the ruling will apply retroactively. The ruling is narrow because it applies only to Ginevan, but Harding said he would be interested in bringing a habeas petition for a similar client under the right circumstances.

“This isn’t a broad, sweeping decision that undermines felon-in-possession laws, but it does invite future defendants, particularly those with histories lacking a crime of violence, to raise Second Amendment arguments,” Harding said in an interview.

The ruling doesn’t change the fact federal law prohibits felons from purchasing firearms. Attorneys representing Ginevan did not respond to a request for comment.

#7534. NYC rent freeze beats landlord challenge

While a state judge upheld the rent freeze, he called the mayor's campaign promises to enact it "reckless and irresponsible."

MANHATTAN (CN) â New York City’s “rent freeze” affecting more than a million apartment units survived landlords’ challenge on Wednesday as a state judge dismissed entirely their lawsuit aimed at blocking the measure.

The Thanksgiving Eve ruling upholds the NYC Rent Guidelines Board’s June 25 order adjusting the annual adjustment for rent stabilized units to 0% for one- and two-year leases that begin between Oct. 1, 2026, and Sept. 30, 2027. The so-called freeze was a core campaign promise for Mayor Zohran Mamdani.

According to the landlords challenging the rent freeze, the mayor packed the board with loyalists who’d carry out his rent-curbing agenda while ignoring rising property operating costs. The city, defending the freeze, said in turn that data shows tenants are financially struggling, and citywide income increases allow landlords to absorb increased costs.

Judge Brendan T. Lantry noted in Wednesday’s ruling that rent regulation is well-established as a “point of contention among building owners and tenants,” and that the city’s rent board “acted in accordance with the law.”

Based on the current record, Lantry said, the landlords’ claims that the board didn’t act independently of the mayor’s office are “without merit.”

But the judge had harsh words for Mamdani’s campaign pledge to freeze the rent, writing, “the court would be remiss not to state that such comments, promises and guarantees to freeze the rent were reckless and irresponsible.”

“The mayor of the city of New York has no authority to unilaterally raise, ‘freeze’ or otherwise adjust the rent of stabilized units in this city âÂ that responsibility is within the power of the board and the board alone,” Lantry continued. “However, without a showing that the board simply adopted Mayor Mamdani’s campaign promise instead of engaging in an evaluation … Mayor Mamdani’s calls to ‘freeze the rent’ are inconsequential to this proceeding.”

That board members share Mamdani’s politics “is of no moment and does not indicate any level of collusion,” the judge said.

Mamdani said in a statement Wednesday that the NYC Law Department had “made clear that the board had acted within its authority and that tenants needed this relief.”

“Today, Judge Lantry affirmed what we knew all along: the Rent Guidelines Board had the authority to deliver for the more than two million New Yorkers who call rent-stabilized apartments home,” the mayor said, calling the ruling a victory for tenants.

“This holiday weekend, more than two million New Yorkers can breathe a little easier,â Mamdani said.

The plaintiff landlords â seven limited liability companies that own rent-stabilized buildings in Brooklyn, Queens, Staten Island and the Bronx â seek to stop the rent freeze and instead implement a rent increase, citing recent statistics that landlordsâ operating costs in the city rose 5.3% in the most recent year and are projected to rise another 4.1%.

Counsel for the landlords includes attorney Randy Mastro, the former top deputy mayor to Mamdaniâs predecessor and top political opponent Eric Adams. The Dechert LLP attorney said he was disappointed by Wednesday’s ruling.

âDespite the economic realities and uncontroverted factual record that this unprecedented rent freeze will have devastating consequences for small landlords throughout our city, the judge deferred to the [Rent Guidelines Board]âs ultimate decision. Therefore, we are continuing to review the ruling and considering next steps,â Mastro said in a statement.

Mastro, who told the press when he resigned after Mamdani’s election that âI will never work for a socialist," is involved in several other suits challenging the rookie mayor’s policies. The litigator recently took another loss in those efforts when a state appeals court dismissed efforts to undo the mayor’s tax on second homes, which targets high-value city properties.

On Wednesday, Mamdani also announced the expansion of a separate rent freeze program, which benefits senior and disabled New Yorkers.

#7533. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson and the arc of the law

In September, Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson received an award named after the late Justice William Brennan, a liberal lion. In her acceptance speech, Jackson discussed Brennan’s role as the Supreme Court became more conservative, noting that he “believed that even his dissents could make a difference and remind the nation that the pursuit of equal justice under law is an ongoing effort.” Jackson indicated that she agreed with that idea, telling the audience that she saw “dissent[s] as more than just a disagreement with the outcome of a case, I see them as an expression of faith in the future and a demonstration of hope.” As she put it, “However desolate the moment feels, we who write for a future age have hope that the noble and collective work of bending the long arc of the law toward justice will continue.”

Since joining the court in the summer of 2022, Jackson has sought to promote her understanding of that view. Although she has been consistently part of the court’s liberal bloc, even among the three Democratic appointees she has forged a unique role. As her invocation of Brennan suggests, it often appears that her goal is not simply to express disagreement with the majority, but to offer an alternative vision and to speak to the public directly – even if she does so without the support of her fellow liberals.

Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

#7530. Moritz family to Ohio State law school: What’s going on with our $30M gift?

Jeffrey Moritz has written in the Columbus Dispatch that his father’s $30 million donation to Ohio State University’s law school has inexplicably fallen and has only provided 12 to 15 scholarships each year. (Image from Shutterstock)

When Michael Moritz donated more than $30 million to Ohio State University’s law school in 2001, he expected that the money would fund four faculty chairs and 30 annual law school scholarships.

But despite that agreement, records from the law school renamed after him show that the fund inexplicably fell from $30 million to $21.9 in less than 15 years, his son Jeffrey Mortiz writes in the Columbus Dispatch. Only 12 to 15 scholarships have been provided annually, he adds.

In the column, Moritz called upon the Ohio legislature to fix this by passing the Endowment Accountability Act, House Bill 751 and Senate Bill 368 by the end of December. The bill states that donors who believe a public university has violated an endowment agreement must first notify the state’s attorney general, who has 180 days to correct course. Donors in Ohio now have no clear way to hold public universities accountable.

A former head of Baker & Hostetler’s corporate practice and director of Cardinal Health, Michael Moritz attended Ohio State’s law school on a full-ride scholarship before graduating in 1958. Less than a year after making his donation, Moritz, 68, was killed by a hit-and-run driver in Naples, Florida.

#7529. The Second Amendment and an "unusually dangerous" approach to dicta

Please note that SCOTUS Outside Opinions constitute the views of outside contributors and do not reflect the opinions of SCOTUSblog or its staff.

On November 10, The New York Times published an article suggesting that a major piece of the Supreme Court’s Second Amendment jurisprudence is premised on a misquote by the late Justice Antonin Scalia in his 2008 majority opinion in D.C v. Heller, in which the court held that there was an individual right to possess firearms. The essence of the piece is that Scalia used the phrase “dangerous and unusual” to describe those weapons not protected by the right to keep and bear arms, attributing this terminology primarily (or perhaps solely) to the 18th century British jurist William Blackstone. Yet Blackstone’s writings instead use the phrase “dangerous or unusual.”

According to the Times piece, “[t]he consequences of Justice Scalia’s use of ‘and’ rather than ‘or’ have been profound”: “Since all guns are dangerous, courts have had to focus instead on determining whether a type of firearm is unusual, often parsing marketing data and consumer surveys to gauge a weapon’s popularity.” Presumably, if Scalia had used the phrase “dangerous or unusual,” it would be easier for legislatures to ban even certain commonly owned firearms because dangerousness alone would be sufficient to bring a category of weapons outside the amendment’s protective sphere.

The Times story has reverberated quickly, with strong backlash from conservative lawyers and scholars. Such disagreements have focused largely on the specific citation Scalia used. Law professor Jonathan Adler, for example, has argued that the citation to Blackstone was one among many, and additional sources that Scalia cited used the “and” formulation. Others have responded that Scalia was anything but sloppy, which would be especially true when it came to such an influential and important source.

Both sides, though, seem to be burying the lede. In my view, this is a story not about historical errors or the nuances of legal citation. Rather, it is about how judicial dicta that was never intended to lay down broad, permanent rules has taken on a life of its own, and how other justices on the Supreme Court subsequently canonized Scalia’s stray language by turning it into a “test” that would govern any number of future cases – when it’s not at all clear Scalia ever contemplated this or would have endorsed any such thing.

As most law students and lawyers are well aware, the holding-dicta distinction is deeply rooted in American jurisprudence: generally speaking, the holding is the analysis necessary to resolve the actual case before the court, and everything else in an opinion is dicta (this comes from the Latin phrase “obiter dictum,” or “said in passing”). Fundamental to that distinction is that dicta, while it may be persuasive, is not precedential. As Chief Justice John Marshall wrote in 1821, the reason for not deferring blindly to dicta is “obvious”:

The late Judge Richard Posner once similarly emphasized the risk that dicta “can be misleading if carelessly lifted from the case-specific contexts in which they were originally uttered … That is why courts in assessing the binding effect of previous decisions distinguish between the dicta, which are the inessential parts of the opinion, and the holding.” Circuits vary in their approach to Supreme Court dicta, generally deferring more heavily to such language when they find it thoroughly considered or supported, but the court is, of course, never bound by its own dicta.

In fact, Scalia himself was no fan of relying heavily on dicta from prior Supreme Court decisions. In a 1993 opinion, he criticized a group of dissenting justices by noting that their position found “support, if at all, only in the dicta of this Court’s opinions.” This was, in Scalia’s view, as good as no support at all. Indeed, Scalia rejected reliance on “drive-by … rulings” not fully considered by the issuing court, even if not purely dicta. In his 2015 decision for the court in Kerry v. Din, Scalia excoriated a proposition advanced in a dissenting opinion as resting solely on “dictum in a footnote” and then observed that “[t]he footnoted dictum that Justice Breyer proposes to elevate to constitutional law is a dangerous doctrine.” He further joined opinions that rejected prior dicta as unprincipled, especially when greater investigation revealed reasons for caution.

Scalia’s position was nuanced – for example, he once joined a dissent by Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg that endorsed reliance on certain dictum as persuasive – yet a cautious approach to dicta is consistent with his broader judicial philosophy as well. He was at times willing to jettison even precedential decisions squarely applicable to the case at hand when those decisions were contrary to original public meaning. Unconsidered dicta, presumably, would then be far lower in the pecking order.

Returning to Heller and the phrase at issue, it’s hard to argue that the “dangerous and unusual” passage from Heller is anything but dicta. The issue in Heller was whether a Washington, D.C. ordinance “generally prohibit[ing] the possession of handguns” violated the Second Amendment, or if there was an individual right to keep arms for one’s self-defense. Scalia’s majority opinion answered in the affirmative, as “the American people have considered the handgun to be the quintessential self-defense weapon.” D.C. never argued that handguns were entirely exempt from protection because they were especially dangerous. The question of dangerous and/or unusual weapons was not at issue in the case; accordingly, it wasn’t thoroughly investigated through the adversarial process.

Rather, after canvassing the historical evidence and concluding it supported an individual-rights view of the Second Amendment, Scalia turned to the nature of the right he had just explicated. In three short paragraphs not necessary to the holding, he explained why the amendment did not authorize gun keeping-and-carrying by anyone in any circumstance; rather history revealed limitations on the right, such as “the carrying of ‘dangerous and unusual weapons.’”

Whatever the purpose of this section – Justice John Paul Stevens later suggested the language was proposed by Justice Anthony Kennedy (the crucial fifth vote in Heller) in exchange for joining the majority – it was far from necessary to resolve the case at hand.

So how did such dicta become relevant? In the 2016 case Caetano v. Massachusetts, decided after Scalia had passed away, the justices unanimously overturned a Massachusetts Supreme Court decision upholding that state’s ban on stun guns in a criminal prosecution of a woman who used this weapon to defend herself from an abusive ex-boyfriend. Justice Samuel Alito issued a concurring opinion (joined by Justice Clarence Thomas) that performed an interesting maneuver. Seizing on the fact that the per curiam opinion in that case referenced Scalia’s “dangerous and unusual” formulation, Alito turned Scalia’s language into a doctrinal test: “As the per curiam opinion recognizes, this is a conjunctive test: A weapon may not be banned unless it is both dangerous and unusual.” But the per curiam had done no such thing; rather, that opinion simply cited the passage in Heller as referring to one limitation on the right to keep and bear arms. And the per curiam said that the lower court in that case had faltered by concluding that any weapon not in common use in 1791 was per se unusual, not by failing to use a conjunctive test.

(Ironically, Alito has his own well-publicized objections to giving past Supreme Court dicta undue veneration – his opinion for the court in Dobbs heavily suggested that Roe’s viability framework was entitled to less weight in the stare decisis analysis because it was initially mere dicta, “the Court’s own brainchild [for which n]either party advocated.”)

From there, the “dangerous and unusual” language took on a life of its own. In 2022’s New York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen, in which the court struck down New York’s concealed-carry law, the majority set forth a test for Second Amendment constitutionality privileging historical evidence above all else. At the first step of that test, a court determines whether the conduct at issue is protected by the right to keep and bear arms, which is where the exclusion of dangerous and/or unusual weapons becomes relevant. If the banned weapon is not protected by the Second Amendment (for, say, being “dangerous and unusual”), a constitutional challenge is dead on arrival. If, on the other hand, the plaintiff can show the weapons are protected, then the burden switches to the government to provide historical evidence to support its regulation. (The consequences may be even greater, as some have argued that “usualness” (or “common use”) conclusively establishes not only threshold protection for the weapon but also that any legislative ban is ahistorical and thus unconstitutional.)

This test has divided the judiciary in recent years. For example, a Massachusetts federal judge evaluating a challenge to that state’s AR-15 ban recognized the apparent disconnect between Heller and Blackstone but nevertheless noted that “the Supreme Court has expressly stated . . .that the relevant tradition is one of regulating ‘dangerous and unusual weapons.’” The Massachusetts judge found these weapons were not in “common use,” and, in any event, a historical tradition of responding to technological advances by regulating specific weapons supported the ban. By contrast, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit interpreted Scalia’s language to signal that widespread ownership of AR-15s and large-capacity magazines meant any legislative attempt to ban them was unconstitutional. The “dangerous and unusual” framework has led other judges on a search for ownership statistics and sales data to assess a weapon’s popularity, triggering sharp debate over whether a test that ultimately turns on commonality is even workable.

This is particularly relevant since the court is currently preparing to hear oral argument in Viramontes v. Cook County, a Second Amendment challenge to state and local bans on AR-15s, on December 2. While the recent attention to Scalia’s citation may trigger discussion at oral argument, most justices are now likely to treat “dangerous and unusual” as an established standard and ownership statistics as definitive proof that AR-15s are not unusual and thus protected. Absent from this, however, will be the fact that this standard did not emerge from any well-reasoned, litigation-tested analysis making it deserve deference in the first place – especially under Scalia’s own approach to judging.

The debate over Scalia’s Blackstone citation, then, has obscured a more important problem: the Supreme Court’s decision to treat its past dicta as doctrine that can settle the outcome of cases on which the court has never passed.

Andrew Willinger is an Assistant Professor at Georgia State University College of Law, where he teaches constitutional law and civil procedure.

#7524. California sees record high tides, but limited damage

The king tides caused big waves, but little more than minor flooding.

(CN) âÂ Several beaches along the coast of Southern California saw record high tides Wednesday, thanks to the convergence of three factors: the astronomical event known as “king tides,” the “El NiÃ±o” climate cycle, and global warming.

Preliminary data measured high tide at the Los Angeles Harbor, in the San Pedro neighborhood, at 8.19 feet, tying the previous record of about a month ago, with records going all the way back to 1923. La Jolla and Santa Barbara had all-time record high tides, though the data for Santa Barbara only goes as far back as 1990.

State and local officials, including Governor Gavin Newsom, had warned extensive flooding could disrupt travel plans and flood coastal communities. Those fears appear not to have been fully realized. Todd Hall, a meteorologist at the National Weather Service’s Los Angeles office in Oxnard, said said that the two factors prevented the tides from being worse: a storm surge in Northern California that petered out, and the fact that high tide and large swells took place at different times of day.

“There is some reprieve, because the high tide this morning, surf and swell coming up into tonight,” Hall said. “Things would be much worse if we had high surf arriving at the same time we had high tide.”

Some areas did see minor flooding. Streets were underwater in the low-lying neighborhood of Sunset Beach in Huntington Beach this morning. Meanwhile, in the Bay Area, water from San Francisco Bay spilled onto the Embarcadero, and in Pacifica massive waves destroyed a section of the municipal pier. Santa Cruz County and Marin County both issued evacuation warnings for homes along the coast, though the latter has already been lifted.

Warnings and advisories remain in place up and down the coast, but so far, the king tides have been less destructive than feared.

“It is a relief, that things weren’t worse,” said Febe Rothenberg, meteorologist at the National Weather Service in San Francisco. Still, she warned: “Pretty please, avoid the beach.”

King tides, also called perigean spring tides, are predictable astronomical events that occur when a new or full moon lines up with both the sun and Earth. The gravitational pull of the three bodies combine and cause exceptionally high tides. On The next king tide will be a month from now, on Christmas Eve, when tides could be even higher if a storm hits.

This year’s especially strong El NiÃ±o means surface waters in the Pacific Ocean have been unusually warm, causing higher-than-average tides, larger waves and more frequent storms.

In general, scientists predict tides will be higher and higher, thanks global warming, which has melted glaciers and caused ocean levels to rise three-to-four inches in the last 30 years.

WASHINGTON (CN) â A federal judge on Wednesday blocked the Federal Communications Commission from acting on its threat to revoke ABC News of its broadcasting license, finding the early revocation for the national broadcaster and eight regional affiliates would clearly chill their speech.

U.S. District Judge Loren AliKhan granted the news agencyâs motion for a preliminary injunction to halt the ongoing license renewal process and denied the Justice Departmentâs motion to dismiss the case on jurisdictional grounds.

âThis is not a close case,â the Joe Biden appointee wrote inÂ her 45-page opinion. âNo one doubts that the commission may enforce the law in the manner it sees fit. But in doing so, defendants may not retaliate against or punish plaintiffs or other broadcast license holders for disfavored speech.â

âPlaintiffs have a weighty interest in âvindicating the[ir] right to be free of retaliation for [their] protected speech. And âthere is always a strong public interest in the exercise of free speech rights otherwise abridged by an unconstitutionalâ government action.â

AliKhan rejected the governmentâs argument that the license renewal was inherently tied to an initial March 2025 anti-discrimination probe into Disneyâs hiring practices â part of the Justice Departmentâs ongoing campaign to roll back diversity, equity and inclusion practices â and the companyâs refusal to provide requested documents.

âIf defendants initiated the early license renewal proceedings to punish plaintiffs for their protected expression, then it is irrelevant whether defendants could conjure up an adequate basis to investigate plaintiffs or subsequently deny their licenses,â AliKhan wrote. âAs plaintiffs put it, they âdo not ask whether there was any violation of FCC rules,â but instead bring a textbook retaliation claim that is well suited for judicial resolution.â

Beth Wilkinson, of Wilkinson Stekloff and attorney for ABC News, described the FCCâs threats to a hanging guillotine, the falling of which would amount to a âcorporate death penalty.â

âAny broadcaster of ordinary firmness â wealthy or not â would not hesitate to think twice if faced with such an existential threat to its business,â AliKhan wrote, rejecting the Trump administrationâs assertion that the Disney Company could not be readily intimidated due to its wealth.

The Justice Department argued the FCC was obligated to initiate the anti-discrimination investigation, as regulated entities and trustees of the nationâs public airwaves must serve the public interest.

At an Oct. 6 hearing, Justice Department attorney Dimitar Georgiev-Remmel highlighted President Donald Trumpâs July 16 national address from the White House, where he advanced baseless claims of election fraud, that ABC News and NBC News declined to broadcast as proof the outlet was not acting in the public interest.

AliKhan further rejected the governmentâs argument that the broadcaster could only seek relief in the D.C. Circuit over concerns that any action taken by AliKhan would undermine her and the appellate courtâs jurisdictions. She noted that any such challenge would only come after an FCC denial, and if the FCC renews the licenses, then the broadcaster would have no First Amendment retaliation claim.

The FCCâs license review of ABC News and eight of its regional affiliates â the stationâs licenses were set to expire between December 2028 and August 2031 â is the first use of the process in nearly 60 years, Wilkinson said. She added that, even if the FCC decides to ultimately grant their renewals, the guillotine blade remains hanging over the news outletâs head throughout the process, which clearly chills its First Amendment activity.

The Disney CompanyÂ sued the Trump administration on Aug. 18, seeking an order blocking the FCC from issuing a hearing designation order, where the company anticipated its renewal applications or licenses could be revoked.

The company highlighted how the âJimmy Kimmel Live!â late show was temporarily suspended last year following the comedianâs comments regarding the assassination of right-wing debater Charlie Kirk suggesting the GOP sought to âscore political pointsâ off his death.

ABC temporarily suspended Kimmelâs show for five days hours after Carr issued an ultimatum that âwe can do this the easy way or the hard way.â

That same week, the FCC ordered ABCâs eight regional stations to file early applications for license renewal, years before the usual time for such renewals and allowing just 30 days to file applications that usually take months.

The stations include affiliates in Durham, North Carolina, Chicago, Houston, Los Angeles, San Francisco, New York, Philadelphia and Fresno, California. For all but the Durham and Chicago stations, the review comes before their current licenses have reached the halfway mark.

ABC and the FCC did not respond to a request for comment.

#7521. What do these Supreme Court plaintiffs have in common?

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

Each weekday, we present news articles and commentary related to the Supreme Court in a smart, approachable way.

Free readers receive the Friday edition. Full access is for members.

A written companion to Advisory Opinions, bringing together each episode’s key arguments, takeaways, show notes, and source material on the Supreme Court, the Constitution, and the law.

Coverage and analysis of Supreme Court opinion announcements.

Professor Akhil Reed Amar, joined by co-host Andy Lipka, offers weekly in-depth discussions on the most urgent and fascinating constitutional issues of our day.

Divided Argument is an unscheduled, unpredictable Supreme Court podcast hosted by Will Baude and Dan Epps.

Last term in Little v. Hecox, which concerned whether states could bar transgender female athletes from participating in girl’s and women’s sports, Justice Sonia Sotomayor asked Idaho Solicitor General Alan Hurst: “Do you dispute that having a case named after you makes your infamy ... live forever? ... You don't think that Brown and any of the other named plaintiffs that we have in famous cases dr[ew] … attention to those people as people?” Sotomayor asked the question in the context of Hecox requesting that the Supreme Court dismiss the case, citing, in part, “negative public scrutiny ... because of this litigation.”

On Tuesdays for the past few months, we have dedicated the “Closer Look” section of SCOTUSblog’s daily newsletter to covering the story of some of the most famous plaintiffs behind landmark Supreme Court cases.

Now 16 installments in, we thought it would be a good time to take a step back and assess what’s been learned. In this article, we offer a glimpse at the lives of a baker, a farmer, an executive director at Planned Parenthood, two students, and a leader of the Ku Klux Klan. But besides having interesting (and sometimes disturbing) life stories, what do they all have in common? Each asked the Supreme Court to answer one of the most fundamental questions of all: Where does government power end and personal liberty begin?

Let’s start with Joseph Lochner. Lochner immigrated from Bavaria, Germany, to the United States at the age of 20 in 1882, and settled in Utica, New York. He sought employment in the bakery industry; around 1890, he opened his own small, family bakeshop in Utica.

During this time, efforts emerged across New York to regulate the conditions of bakery workers after an article written by Edward Marshall, a muckraker, revealed their unsanitary conditions. In 1895, the state passed The Bakeshop Act, which aimed to prevent biscuit, cake, and bread bakers from working more than 10 hours a day or 60 hours a week.

Twice charged with violating this statute, Lochner decided to challenge the law on the grounds that it violated the 14th Amendment’s Due Process Clause, which he argued protected the economic liberty to enter into such a contract with one’s employees.

Lochner ultimately made its way to the Supreme Court and presented the court with the question of whether New York’s law violated Lochner’s fundamental liberty interest. Everyone agreed that, under the powers reserved to the states, New York certainly had some powers to regulate general welfare. The question was whether New York had gone too far in restricting an employer’s freedom to contract with his employees.

For some, the New York statute was perfectly legitimate and a function of the democratic process. As then-future Judge Learned Hand argued, “we should not have the inconsistent spectacle of a government, in theory representative, which distrusted the courage and justice of its representatives, and put its faith in a [judiciary] which was, and ought to be, the least representative of popular feeling." Put simply, if there was a legitimate legislative purpose for the law, then according to Hand, courts should defer to what the elected representatives decided.

In what was seen even at the time as a surprising decision, the Supreme Court sided with Lochner five to four. “The general right to make a contract in relation to his business is part of the liberty of the individual protected by the Fourteenth Amendment of the Federal Constitution,” wrote Justice Rufus Peckham in his majority opinion.

While Peckham conceded there could be grounds for the legislature to implement regulations to improve workplace safety, he also held there was not sufficient evidence that the Bakeshop Act’s hour-limits would actually improve worker health. And if the statute was upheld, Peckham argued that it would open up almost every aspect of life to state regulation.

In dissent, Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes lampooned the majority, writing that “a constitution is not intended to embody a particular economic theory.”

Lochner has since been abandoned and its reasoning rejected by most legal scholars. Yet defenders remain. Law Professor Randy Barnett, for example, argues for a theory that if the government wants to institute a regulation of liberty, “the burden of proof is more or less on the legislature.” This gets at a fundamental debate in constitutional law: Why do certain civil liberties not explicitly mentioned in the Constitution get heightened scrutiny while economic liberty does not?

As for Lochner himself, he returned to private life and continued to run his bakery. He died on December 14, 1939.

Few cases are more detested by constitutional conservatives than Wickard v. Filburn. Roscoe Curtiss Filburn was born on August 2, 1902, in Dayton, Ohio. A fifth-generation farmer, Filburn grew crops and raised livestock. The crops included winter wheat, which was, in part, for personal use.

In a New Deal effort to help prop up the struggling agriculture industry, Congress enacted the Agricultural Adjustment Act of 1938. The secretary of Agriculture would create a national allotment of acres that could be used to produce wheat. The allotment would then be appropriated to states and ultimately to individual farmers. Filburn’s allotment in 1940 was for 11.1 acres of wheat, but he planted 23 acres of it. Administrators of the AAA fined Filburn 49 cents per excess bushel that he grew and placed a lien of $117.11 on his entire wheat yield.

Filburn challenged the excess penalty in court on the grounds that the statute was passed under the Commerce Clause, which states that Congress shall have the power to “regulate Commerce ... among the several States.” Filburn contended that his activities did not implicate interstate commerce.

If the winter wheat was grown by Filburn and never crossed state lines, could Congress then regulate it?

The Supreme Court sided against Filburn, holding unanimously that his economic activities, taken in the aggregate, would have a substantial effect on interstate commerce. The logic went as follows: If Filburn grew his own wheat, then he would not need to purchase wheat on the open market; and if many farmers did this, it would undermine Congress’ efforts to stabilize the price of crops. “That [Filburn’s] own contribution to the demand for wheat may be trivial by itself is not enough to remove him from the scope of federal regulation where, as here, his contribution, taken together with that of many others similarly situated, is far from trivial,” explained Justice Robert Jackson.

The decision remains controversial to this day (to put it mildly). Critics of Filburn argue that the decision gives Congress near unlimited power to enact regulations under the Commerce Clause, effectively allowing Congress to regulate every aspect of people’s lives and largely mooting the powers reserved to the states. In the late 1990s and early 2000s, the Supreme Court appeared ready to reduce the Commerce Clause’s reach, striking down two statutes as exceeding Congress’ power. But it has not invalidated a law on these grounds since. (Although the Supreme Court in National Federation of Independent Business v. Sebelius held that Congress lacked the power to enact the Affordable Care Act’s individual mandate under the Commerce Clause, it ultimately upheld the mandate under Congress’ power to tax.)

Filburn returned to private life after his Supreme Court case and rarely spoke about it. During the 1950s, he purchased Beverly Shop, a woman’s beauty store, and, in 1966, Filburn convinced the other successors to his grandparent’s 640-acre farm to collectively sell the land to developers. He died on October 4, 1987, at the age of 85.

Estelle Griswold: Griswold v. Connecticut

Estelle Griswold was born on June 8, 1900, in Hartford, Connecticut. A talented singer, she attended The Hartt School of Music, a music conservatory in Hartford. In 1935, she moved to Washington, D.C. for her husband’s job, where she volunteered at a doctor’s office and worked at George Washington University as a lab instructor.

In the 1950s, Griswold moved to New Haven and a few years later was offered the role of executive director of the Planned Parenthood League of Connecticut. In 1961, she opened a birth control clinic in New Haven, along with a doctor, but was convicted and fined $100 in violation of the Barnum Act, a Connecticut law that prohibited the use of “any drug, medicine, article, or instrument” to prevent conception (and, yes, named after that Barnum).

Soon after the decision was announced, the PPLC clinic reopened, but Griswold stepped down as executive director as she had fallen out of favor with some members of the organization due to its continued financial struggles. Griswold passed away on August 13, 1981, in Fort Myers, Florida at age 81 and was posthumously inducted into the Connecticut Women’s Hall of Fame in 1994.

Another major area of constitutional controversy has involved the limits of free speech in the classroom context. Although such cases continue to crop up (BONG HiTS 4 JESUS, anyone?), the modern foundation for them was laid in 1969’s Tinker v. Des Moines. Which brings us to the Tinkers.

John Tinker was born in 1950, and his sister, Mary Beth, was born in 1952. They grew up in Atlantic, Iowa, where their father was the pastor of a Methodist church. In November 1965, John, then a high schooler, attended a rally in opposition to the Vietnam War in Washington, D.C. On the way back to Iowa, John and other protesters agreed to wear black armbands to protest the war and to mourn the deaths on both sides.

More than 50 students across public schools in Des Moines planned to wear black armbands to school on December 16, 1965, in support of Sen. Robert Kennedy’s proposed Christmas truce. However, local principals instituted a policy that all students wearing black armbands would be asked to remove them.

On December 16, 1965, Mary Beth wore a black armband to Warren Harding Junior High School and was suspended after she refused to take it off. The next day, John wore a black armband to North High School and was also suspended after declining to remove it.

In March 1966, the Tinkers sued, arguing the schools violated their constitutional rights. Specifically, the Tinkers contended that the public schools were an arm of the state and they were therefore bound by the First Amendment.

Allan Herrick, arguing for Des Moines at the Supreme Court, contended that the school district must be in a position to “preserve order and to avoid this disturbance and disruption in the school room.” As Justice Thomas would argue decades later in Morse v. Frederick, “through the legal doctrine of in loco parentis [in the place of a parent], courts [historically] upheld the right of schools to discipline students, to enforce rules, and to maintain order.”

In February 1969, the Supreme Court sided with the Tinkers, holding that students do not “shed their constitutional rights to freedom of speech or expression at the schoolhouse gate.” In its decision, written by Justice Abe Fortas, the court established the substantial disruption test, which sets the necessary conditions for regulating student speech. To do so, the school must be able to reasonably foretell “material and substantial interference” with other students’ learning or the school’s operations. Fortas held that the school district failed to show that the Tinkers’ protests resulted in any material disruption.

To this day, Tinker receives mixed reviews. Supporters of an expansive interpretation of the First Amendment tend to support the principles in Tinker and argue that they should be even more broadly applied; critics, such as Justice Thomas, are skeptical that students have First Amendment rights at all. (As Justice Hugo Black put it in his Tinker dissent, “It may be that the Nation has outworn the old-fashioned slogan that ‘children are to be seen, not heard,’ but one may, I hope, be permitted to harbor the thought that taxpayers send children to school on the premise that, at their age, they need to learn, not teach.”).

After the Supreme Court’s decision, John Tinker remained active in anti-Vietnam war demonstrations and later became the manager of KPIP-LP 94.7 FM, a local radio station, which he manages to this day. Mary Beth Tinker pursued a career in medicine, working as a pediatric and emergency room nurse and a nurse practitioner. In 2013, Mary Beth left the nursing field and embarked on the “Tinker Tour,” where she travels the country telling her story and promoting civic education to young people.

Clarence Brandenburg: Brandenburg v. Ohio

Let’s conclude with our least likable plaintiff, who nevertheless established one of the most enduring Supreme Court precedents. Clarence Brandenburg was born on March 3, 1916, in Lee County, Kentucky. A Marine Corps veteran, he worked at a General Electric plant and operated a television repair shop upon returning to civilian life. After declaring personal bankruptcy in 1959, Brandenburg began getting involved with white supremacist organizations and sought to become a leader of the KKK.

In June 1964, Brandenburg spoke at a Klan rally, which was shown on a local television station. Brandenburg said “We're not a revengent organization, but if our President, our Congress, our Supreme Court, continues to suppress the white, Caucasian race, it's possible that there might have to be some revengeance taken. ... We are marching on Congress July the Fourth, four hundred thousand strong.” He was then charged with violating Ohio’s criminal syndicalism statute prohibiting advocating “sabotage, violence, or ... terrorism ... as a means of accomplishing ... political reform,” and later convicted.

Brandenburg appealed, arguing that his speech was protected by the First Amendment. Specifically, he argued that Ohio could not punish him for advocating for unlawful action without showing that his speech was directed towards producing such action.

Leonard Kirschner, arguing on behalf of Ohio at the Supreme Court, asserted that Brandenburg’s actions were not conducted in isolation and could lead to violence, contending that “the statements [made by Brandenburg] to 10 or 20 people can cause one heck of a lot of crime and violence and terrorism in any community. It only takes one person to cause it.”

The Supreme Court reversed Brandenburg’s conviction in 1969 on First Amendment grounds. According to the court, the Ohio statute in question failed to distinguish between an abstract endorsement of unlawful activity and speech directed towards producing imminent, lawless action. In doing so, the court established what became known as the Brandenburg test, which required that speech sufficient for incitement be “directed to inciting or producing imminent lawless action” and “likely to incite or produce such action.”

In 1971, Brandenburg was found guilty of harassing his Jewish neighbor by repeatedly calling him and uttering antisemitic slurs. He died on March 29, 1986.

They came from different backgrounds, had very different worldviews, and dealt with different issues, but each of these plaintiffs had one thing in common: pushing up against the limits of state power. How that power manifested itself differed considerably, as did the court’s willingness to reign it in. For example, while the court has advanced a highly protective understanding of the First Amendment, it has been more hesitant to advance protections of economic liberty.

The nature of the plaintiff also mattered less in these cases than one might presume. Filburn was a farmer who grew wheat for his own personal consumption but did not prevail at the court. Brandenburg, on the other hand, expressed white supremacist ideas yet proved successful before the justices, becoming responsible for an entirely new free speech doctrine.

Some may view the court blinding itself to the actual facts on the ground as too simplistic; others as an ideal to aspire to. On that note, we’ll give Justice Elena Kagan the final word: “the question is not do you like this party or do you like that party ... the question is what the law requires.”

LOS ANGELES (CN) â Brad Pitt and Angelina Jolie reached a quiet settlement Wednesday in their legal dispute over Miraval, an estate in the south of France that was their home and the base of their lucrative winemaking operation.

âWe have settled out of court in the best interests of our family and will not be commenting further,â spokespeople for the pair said in a written joint statement. âAny comments in media stories attributed to âsourcesâ are in fact not coming from either of us, or anyone close to us.â

Terms of the settlement were not disclosed.

First filed more than four years ago in February 2022, the lawsuit provided a veritable goldmine for tabloids and celebrity news sites, as the two actors, once the most famous married couple in America, took increasingly nasty swipes at each other in court filings.

In a countersuit, Jolie claimed that Pitt was abusive toward her and and their children, detailing one incident in 2016 aboard a private jet in which Pitt âgrabbed her by the head and shook her,â âchoked one of the childrenâ and âstruck another in the face.â Pitt denied the accusations, which continue to haunt the Hollywood star online.

Jolie and Pitt purchased ChÃ¢teau Miraval in 2008 for $37.5 million through separate holding companies â Pitt’s Mondo Bongo and Jolie’s Nouvel. They would eventually get married at the 1,200-acre estate’s 13th century stone chapel. Pitt became increasingly obsessed with Miraval’s winemaking operation, telling Wine Spectator magazine in 2014, âIâm a farmer now.â Revenues from the company grew from $3 million in 2013 to more than $50 million in 2021.

In 2016, Pitt and Jolie split up. As divorce proceedings wore on, Jolie reached what she called “a painful decision, with a heavy heart.” She wanted to sell her half of Miraval.

She and Pitt nearly reached a deal, for Pitt to buy Jolie out for $54.5 million. But the agreement fell apart at the eleventh hour, according to Jolie’s cross-complaint, over Pittâs demand that she sign a ânon-disparagement clause that would prohibit Jolie from discussing outside of court any of Pittâs personal conduct toward her or the family."

Jolie balked and instead sold out to the Stoli Group, a wine and spirts consortium owned by Russian billionaire Yuri Shefler for $67 million.

Pitt sued, claiming that the two had an unwritten, private agreement not to sell their half of Miraval without the otherâs permission.

âJolieâs breach, if allowed to stand, will deprive Pitt of his right to enjoy his private home â without sharing ownership with a stranger â and to secure his position in the business he built from scratch for the long-term benefit of his family,â Pitt wrote in the complaint.

âPitt is an actor, not a winemaker,â Jolie wrote in the cross-complaint. âHe deals in illusions, not dirt and grapes. During the years that he allegedly âbuiltâ the business, he filmed and appeared in dozens of movies, not to mention making countless promotional appearances, jetting-setting around the world for movie premieres and attending Hollywood parties.â

The case dragged in numerous business partners, including Schefler, and consumed a small army of attorneys, who produced countless amended complaints and demurrers. As of Wednesday, the case had 1,170 filings in its docket, some hundreds of pages long.
